purpose: post-freeze confirmation-bias audit removing repeated source-template boilerplate; does not replace primary independent cohort

judgments.reason: A CPU chip alone did not create a PC market; complete-system constraints and complements were needed, so the component was not collapsed into the realized platform.
No evidence about evaluation being gamed, independent verification, or failure modes of evaluators appears in this trajectory.
The 4004 was designed for a calculator but reused across materially different applications, and generalization was an explicit decisive test.
Routes varied from custom logic to kits to open ecosystem depending on component and complement maturity, so no one fixed method was optimal.
IBM's published interfaces served as explicit, compact, durable state encoding constraint information for compatibility rather than raw history.
General-purpose programmable CPUs and open interfaces added complexity but repaid it by enabling reuse and third-party ecosystem growth.
The shift to an ecosystem changed the future production function, with software and complements increasingly driving further improvement.
Initial calculator-contract scope was corrected by realized demand for complete microcomputers, updating the model from chip-centric to ecosystem-centric.
IBM's technical position did not guarantee lasting control; published open architecture transferred authority to compatible suppliers.
Multiple distinct dimensions such as CPU, memory, I/O, software, interfaces, and distribution diverged, making CPU alone an insufficient proxy.

The decisive tests required actual machine ports, and the record warns that portability never meant zero machine-specific code, so the portable source representation was not silently treated as realized behavior.

University/BSD distributions and actual ports across hardware families independently verified the portability claim, while the notes about device-specific code and fragmentation represent failure modes of a naive portability claim.

Unix was rewritten in C and carried by AT&T/BSD distribution across hardware families, with local source adaptation as a decisive test, showing improvement survived materially different machines than the original.
The decisive test of local source adaptation rather than binary cloning and the recognition of machine-specific device code show that one fixed universal porting method was not assumed.

Source-distributed Unix variants and separated portable interfaces do act as explicit persistent state, but the evidence does not address the claim's distinction from raw accumulated history or provenance.
The record notes that a smaller system could outrun a more ambitious predecessor without being feature-complete, so the added complexity of ambitious systems had to repay itself in value.
The transition made executable systems knowledge portable across machines and institutions, changing the production function so networking and tooling could accumulate later.
The note that portability never meant zero machine-specific code is a correction of an overconfident model against realized ports; actual hardware forced the model to be updated.
AT&T licensing and university/BSD distribution show that technical ability to port source did not automatically grant legal authority to redistribute it.

Decisive tests span performance, local adaptation, and interface separation, and Unix could outrun a feature-complete predecessor, showing distinct value dimensions that cannot be collapsed into one score.
The case explicitly separates logical relation representation from physical storage, with the optimizer bridging them without collapsing the model into a realized plan.
Decisive tests compared optimizer plans against expert hand-crafted paths, verifying practicality and acknowledging early performance skepticism.
SQL and the relational model supported arbitrary set-oriented workloads rather than only one optimized path; physical changes remained hidden from queries.
Cost-based optimization is inherently conditional, selecting physical plans from statistics and current query context rather than a fixed global method.
Transactions, recovery and storage manager maintain compact durable persistent state with relational constraints, not raw accumulated record layouts.
The decisive test that optimizer plans must compete with expert hand-crafted paths directly shows adaptive overhead must repay its cost.
SQL let non-specialists ask new questions without bespoke programs, transforming the future productivity of data analysis.
System R's prototype corrected early performance predictions against realized execution, and statistics adjust cost estimates to observed conditions.
The evidence addresses database implementation and performance, not authority, legitimacy, or safety of consequential actions.
Relational success was judged across usability, optimizer performance, concurrency, recovery and storage—no single proxy score sufficed.

OSI formal standards and protocol specs did not guarantee deployment; actual implementation, operations, and transition were required, so representation was not collapsed into realized Internet functionality.
Demonstrations and conversion tests provided verification, while OSI standardization failed as an evaluation because it omitted deployment, showing that evaluative processes can fail.
TCP/IP routed across packet radio, satellite, and ARPANET without assuming one link behavior, surviving loss and reordering beyond any single network's optimized case.
Rejecting replacement by one universal network in favor of an end-to-end protocol over heterogeneous, independently administered networks shows the method depended on existing conditions.
The evidence lists IP addressing and DNS as complements, but gives no detail about preserving verified causal, provenance, or constraint information versus raw accumulated history.
NCP was a simpler baseline but insufficient; TCP/IP plus deployment and transition overhead repaid that cost by enabling real internetworking across heterogeneous networks.
No source-native evidence ties the internetworking transition to changing the future production function of discovery or improvement; only operational success is shown.
TCP experimentation led to separating IP from transport, and decisive tests corrected the design against realized loss and reordering, showing predictions were updated by observations.
OSI standardization and strong protocols alone did not automatically achieve deployment; host software, addressing, naming, and operations staff were needed to gain real-world admissibility.
Distinct decisive axes such as multi-technology routing, end-to-end semantics, host conversion, and addressing/naming show that one formal standard or proxy could not capture deployment success.
The case concerns building and diffusing the World Wide Web, not the relationship between a proxy/report/metric and realized state. No proxy-vs-reality collapse is depicted.

The decisive tests explicitly include independent servers and clients interoperating without central approval, and the NeXT browser failure was recognized through real usability conditions. This reflects need for verification whose failure modes matter.

The Web generalized from CERN's heterogeneous laboratory setting to common computers and non-specialists globally through portability and cross-platform graphical browsers, surviving materially different conditions beyond the original case.

The route choice depended on world conditions: heterogeneous machines, existing Internet, and competing information systems made open Internet hypertext preferable to central databases, proprietary hypertext, or Gopher menus.
The evidence describes open standards, URLs, and browsers, but does not address an agent's compact persistent state preserving causal/provenance/constraint information versus raw history.
The Web's added complexity over simpler baselines like Gopher menus or a central database was repaid by enormous diffusion and interoperability value, showing added structure must be worthwhile.
The Web became a global platform enabling future inventions and further standard coordination; it changed the production function of information sharing and subsequent discovery.
The case includes real-world tests and corrections such as the NeXT browser not being broadly deployable, but no explicit predictions or prediction-error update mechanism is documented.
The evidence discusses open release and decentralization of control but does not address granting authority, legitimacy, or safety admissibility for consequence-bearing actions.

Multiple decisive criteria were used—cross-machine retrieval, interoperation without central approval, and usability for non-specialists—showing that distinct dimensions were not collapsed into one proxy score.
Case evidence focuses on standards, spectrum, roaming, and interoperability; there is no discussion of proxy/report/metric collapse into realized state.
The case shows verification through conformance testing and multi-supplier interoperability, but it does not represent evaluator gaming or explicit failure modes, narrowing the claim's scope.
GSM's common digital system was adopted by multiple suppliers and expanded beyond Europe, showing the standard generalized beyond its initial European optimized conditions.
No single cellular standard dominated globally, with NMT, AMPS, and CDMA fitting different conditions, so one fixed global standard was not assumed optimal.
The case does not address persistent state design, provenance/history tradeoffs, or compact state storage; standards are not framed in those terms.
Standardization traded local design freedom for larger interoperable markets, showing coordination overhead repaid by greater system value than isolated local optimization.
Standards, conformance testing, SIM/authentication, and supplier ecosystems altered the future production function of mobile telephony by enabling multi-supplier expansion.
Realized demonstrations and decisive tests imply updating from experience, but no explicit prediction-error correction mechanism or world-model update is evidenced.
A capable handset without coverage, roaming, and tariffs had little standalone value, so technical capability alone did not confer usable authority or admissibility.
Decisive tests separately assessed handoff/call setup, interoperability/roaming, spectrum efficiency, and billing/authentication, so multiple value dimensions were not collapsed into one proxy.

Ephemeris/orbit models and signal representations are continuously corrected against observed clock/orbit errors; the model is not collapsed into realized position, and policy limits realized accuracy separately from modeled accuracy.
The case does not address evaluator integrity or gaming of tests; decisive tests concern system accuracy, not verification failure modes.
GPS moved from military design to global civil/receiver diffusion, showing the system survived materially different user conditions; though policy limited civil accuracy, the improvement generalized.
The choice of integrated NAVSTAR over competing routes was conditional on prior system limits and available technology; continuous orbit updates adapt to current conditions.
Ground control maintains compact ephemeris and clock-correction state representing verified orbital dynamics, not raw tracking history.
The added control/timing/user segments were heavy overhead compared to inertial or ground radio, but they repaid by enabling continuous global accuracy sufficient to become infrastructure.
Becoming infrastructure changed the future production function by enabling countless downstream navigation/timing applications and further receiver/technology improvements.
The control segment explicitly estimates and updates clock/orbit errors from tracking observations, correcting prediction models against realized data.
Military/civil authority and policy boundaries determined which users could realize high accuracy, showing technical capability alone did not grant authoritative access.
GPS success depended on distinct axes: ranging accuracy, satellite geometry, clock/orbit updates, receiver affordability, and policy restrictions; no single proxy fully captured operational value.
Cloning success did not establish product safety; hazard risk was distinguished from demonstrated capability, so representation was not collapsed into consequence.
Scientists self-policed by deferring experiments, and products later had to meet regulatory purity requirements, showing verification beyond initial claims.
Recombinant DNA moved from laboratory cloning to industrial production of human proteins, surviving materially different scale and conditions.
Asilomar and NIH chose risk-tiered, contingency-based containment rather than a fixed global ban, so the method was applied conditionally.
NIH guidelines formalized durable containment tiers and responsibilities, encoding constraint information as persistent institutional state.
The temporary pause and institutional oversight cost immediate freedom but preserved a path to continued research and industrialization, repaying overhead.
Recombinant DNA became an industrial biotech platform, changing the future production function for human proteins and further discovery.
Initial risk uncertainty was corrected through staged containment choices as research proceeded; cloning success did not override actual safety evidence.
Cloning capability did not automatically confer safety or manufacturing authority; ownership and authority questions arose separately from laboratory biosafety.
Product purity, biosafety containment, and ownership/authority were distinct dimensions; cloning success alone did not settle them.

The conceptual amplification loop and early manual success were representations distinct from the realized automated platform; early results did not predict throughput without complements, showing representation should not be collapsed into reality.
Contamination was a failure mode that could make amplification evidence misleading, so decisive claims required contamination controls and specificity verification for high-stakes use.

The platform had to remain robust through repeated thermal cycles and manage contamination in high-stakes uses, not just show initial sequence-specific amplification, demonstrating generalization beyond the optimized first demonstration.
The case lists candidate routes but does not show that a chosen method was conditional on evidence or that a fixed global method was rejected as non-optimal; no data on conditional policy.
The PCR history concerns an amplification platform and gives no evidence about persistent state representation, provenance, or compact memory preserving verified information.

Thermostable polymerase and cycling automation added complexity but were necessary for routine many-cycle PCR, so the added overhead repaid itself by enabling a practical platform beyond manual cycling.
PCR became an instrument-like platform and diffused into cloning, diagnostics, sequencing and forensics, changing the production function of future molecular discovery and application.
Manual early success was corrected by realized observations showing it did not predict throughput; the practical platform required thermostable enzyme and automation, updating the conceptual model.
Amplification capability alone did not make results safe or admissible for high-stakes forensic and diagnostic use; contamination controls and primer specificity practices were required.

Decisive success required multiple distinct dimensions: sequence-specific exponential amplification, robustness through thermal cycles, and contamination/specificity control, not a single proxy score.
Proof-of-principle images were far from a hospital scanner, showing reconstructed representations were not collapsed into realized clinical state.
Decisive tests represented failure modes—SNR, artifacts, safety—rather than trusting initial images as sufficient verification.
Spatial encoding generalized from small-sample proof to whole-body clinical MRI under different magnet, RF and workflow conditions.
MRI's value was conditional: CT remained superior for some tasks, so the method was not treated as globally optimal.
The case evidence does not address persistent state/provenance/constraint storage, only engineering and clinical components.
No explicit cost-benefit comparison of added gradient/echo-planar complexity against a simpler baseline is provided in the evidence.
Spatial encoding opened the imaging frontier and enabled later rapid gradient/echo-planar methods, changing the discovery production function.
Observed scan time, SNR, artifacts and safety corrected expectations, and CT superiority for some tasks updated the model of MRI's role.
Technical imaging capability did not automatically grant clinical admissibility; whole-body safety, reliability and protocols had to be verified.
Success depended on multiple divergent axes—soft-tissue contrast, speed, SNR, safety—not a single proxy score.
The case distinguishes the locally maximal energy-density metric from the realized state of safe cycle life; the early high-energy cell failed in realized cycling and fire tests.
Initial lab demonstration was not decisive; repeated cycling and abuse tests exposed dendrite/fire failure modes, so viability claims had to be verified with failure modes represented.

The commercial cell had to survive repeated cycling, manufacturing, and abuse conditions, not just its optimized laboratory energy-density condition; lithium-metal cells failed these materially different conditions.

Route choice was conditional on observed safety and cycling evidence: metallic lithium was rejected after dendrite observations, and a carbon-host/oxide-cathode architecture was adopted instead of a fixed globally optimal design.
The evidence concerns physical materials, architecture selection, and safety testing, with no information about persistent information-state design or preserving provenance in a compact state.

Added material and control corrections that eliminated metallic lithium reduced local energy density but repaid cost by making safe cycling and commercial manufacturability possible, unlike the simpler unsafe high-energy baseline.

No source-native evidence addresses whether the improvement changed the future production function of discovery; portable-electronics demand appears only as external pressure, not as a metaproductive effect.

Expectations from initial intercalation demonstrations were corrected against realized repeated-cycling failures, leading to the carbon-anode architecture; observations, not the model, dictated the safe design.

Technical capability to build high-energy metallic-lithium cells did not make them admissible for commercial use; safety and abuse testing had to be passed, so capability did not confer consequence-bearing authority.

Energy density and safety/cycle life were distinct axes that diverged: the highest-energy option failed safety tests, while the commercial design traded some energy density for cyclability and safety.
Measurements and models were uncertain, and independent measurements were needed to distinguish real depletion from instrument artifact, so representations were not collapsed into reality.
Independent confirmation and measurement checks were decisive; the case stresses that neither one paper nor one treaty explains the correction, and data artifacts had to be ruled out.
The dramatic Antarctic signal was not treated as the only target; controls were made international, remained feasible across countries and industries, and adapted as evidence and substitutes changed.

The route shifted from continued use to national controls, then an international framework, then binding controls with later strengthening as evidence and substitute availability changed, showing condition-dependent method choice.
The case shows long-term monitoring, assessments, and reporting mattered, but it does not clarify whether useful state was compact or merely raw accumulated history.

The added complexity of monitoring, assessments, international framework, and treaty compliance repaid itself by enabling adaptive controls after the Antarctic discovery; simple national measures alone were insufficient.

Long-term monitoring and assessment infrastructure changed future discovery and policy production, enabling the Antarctic signal to be recognized and leading to stronger controls; neither one paper nor one treaty caused the correction.

Molina and Rowland's prediction was checked against realized Antarctic measurements, the strongest empirical signal appeared after the hypothesis, and treaty commitments changed with observations and substitutes.

CFCs were technically useful and stable, but that capability did not grant safe admissibility; a delayed global externality resulted, showing technical capability does not confer authority for consequence-bearing action.

CFC utility and ozone protection were distinct value dimensions that diverged; the correction required coupling chemistry, monitoring, substitutes, and adaptive policy rather than optimizing a single proxy.
